Question #1:

Compare m1 and m2 above. Both were built from 1:9 with nrow = 3, ncol = 3, but they look different.
Explain exactly what byrow = TRUE changes about how R fills a matrix.
(Your answer here)
> Answer: m1 fills the matrix column by column (default behavior) while
m2 fills the matrix row by row because of byrow = TRUE.


Question #2

If you tried matrix(1:8, nrow = 3, ncol = 3) (only 8 numbers for 9 slots), what do you think would happen?
Test it and explain the result, including any warning message.
(Your answer here)
```{r}
numbers <- matrix(1:8, nrow = 3, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)

colnames(numbers) <- c("Aba", "Bab", "Cab")
rownames(numbers) <- c("1", "2", "3")

print(numbers)
```
> Answer: The r program automatically fills out the missing element/number by repeating it from the first number. The code still works.

Question #3

scores[1, ] and scores[, "Ben"] both return a result, but one represents a row and the other a column.
Run class() on each result. What data structure does R “downgrade” a single row/column of a matrix to, and why do you think R does this automatically?
(Your answer here)

```{r}
scores <- matrix(c(88, 92, 79, 95, 84, 90), nrow = 2, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
rownames(scores) <- c("Quiz1", "Quiz2")
colnames(scores) <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid")

scores[1, ]
class(scores)

scores[, "Ben"]
class(scores)
```

> Answer: R automatically changes a single row or column of a matrix into a vector. 
          It does this because a single row or column is just a simple list of numbers, so R makes it easier to use and perform calculations.
          In simple terms, R turns the matrix result into a vector because it only contains one row or one column.

Question #4

> Answer: Because the program will just display the values that meets the condition, not the whole matrix.

Question #5

a * b and a %*% b both “multiply” the same two matrices but give different results.
Explain the difference between element-wise multiplication and matrix multiplication in your own words.
(Your answer here)
> Answer: Simple multiplication '*' only multiplies the numbers that are corrresponding with each other meanwhile the true matrix multiplication multiplies rowsby column and then adds the product, getting the proper answer in multiplying matrices.


Question #6

t(scores) swaps rows and columns. Look at dim(scores) versus dim(scores_t).
Why must the row/column names also swap positions when you transpose a matrix?
(Your answer here)

```{r}
scores <- matrix(c(88, 92, 79, 95, 84, 90),
                 nrow = 2, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
rownames(scores) <- c("Quiz1", "Quiz2")
colnames(scores) <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid")

print(scores)
scores_t <- t(scores)
print(scores_t)
dim(scores)
dim(scores_t)

rownames(scores_t)
colnames(scores_t)
```
> Answer: The names switch because the positions of the rows and columns are reversed when we transpose a matrix.

Question #7 * What would happen if you tried cbind(scores, c(85, 91, 100)) — giving 3 values for a matrix that only has 2 rows? * Test it, read the warning/error, and explain why cbind() and rbind()) require matching dimensions.

(Your answer here)

```{r}
scores<- matrix(c(83, 91, 100), nrow = 2, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
cbind(scores, c(83, 91, 100))
rbind(scores, c(83, 91, 100))
```
> Answer: The code produces an error because the scores matrix has 2 rows, while the new vector has 3 values. The cbind() function requires the same number of rows when adding a column. This is why their dimensions must match.

Question #8

In what situation would you use rbind() instead of cbind() when updating a dataset over time?
Give a concrete example (e.g., daily sales, weekly attendance) and explain your reasoning.
(Your answer here)

> Answer: I would use rbind whenever I tally sales so i can add the daily sales in rows. And I will use cbind when i have new information that i can add in columns.

Question #9

A matrix needs 2 indices (scores[row, col]) but an array needs 3 (arr[row, col, layer]).
Using dim(arr), explain in your own words what each of the three numbers represents.
(Your answer here)

> Answer: The array has 2 rows, 3 columns, and 2 layers, which means it contains two 2D matrices stacked together.

Part F — Critical Thinking Challenge
class_a <- matrix(c(85, 90, 78, 92), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
                   dimnames = list(c("S1", "S2"), c("Midterm", "Final")))
class_b <- matrix(c(88, 84, 95, 91), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
                   dimnames = list(c("S3", "S4"), c("Midterm", "Final")))

# TODO: Combine class_a and class_b into one matrix called all_students
# using the correct bind function (think about whether these represent
# new STUDENTS or new SCORE COLUMNS before choosing cbind or rbind)
(Your answer here)

```{r}
class_a <- matrix(
  c(85, 90, 78, 92), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE, 
  dimnames = list(c("S1", "S2"), c("Midterm", "Final")))

class_b <- matrix(
  c(88, 84, 95, 91), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
  dimnames = list(c("S3","S4"),
                  c("Midterm", "Final")))

allstudents <- rbind(class_a, class_b)
print(allstudents)
```



# TODO: From all_students, compute each student's average score across
# Midterm and Final. Hint: rowMeans(all_students) does this in one line.
(Your answer here)
```{r}
class_a <- matrix(
  c(85, 90, 78, 92), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE, 
  dimnames = list(c("S1", "S2"), c("Midterm", "Final")))

class_b <- matrix(
  c(88, 84, 95, 91), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
  dimnames = list(c("S3","S4"),
                  c("Midterm", "Final")))

allstudents <- rbind(class_a, class_b)

rowMeans(allstudents)

```
